Job satisfaction is a standard indicator of well-being at work, but a satisfaction rating also depends on the person who gives it. Data from the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills for employees in `r nC` countries are used to estimate the subjective reward to the Big Five personality traits, defined as job satisfaction net of pay. It is then tested whether this reward comes from better jobs or from how workers report the jobs they have. One standard deviation of emotional stability is associated with about a third of the satisfaction difference between the bottom and top pay deciles. The premium changes little when occupation is held fixed. In a causal mediation analysis with pay held fixed, reported working conditions account for a median of only `r { u <- acm("all", "EMOS"); u <- u[u$total_p < .05, ]; pc(median(u$share)) }`% of it. Each reported condition is split into the mean report of the worker's occupation-by-industry group and the worker's deviation from that mean. Traits are associated with the deviations, while the group means are statistically equivalent across traits. Less stable workers report more demands and also more resources than colleagues in the same jobs. The premium is concentrated in low depression, and trait-by-condition interactions are small. Personality composition accounts for about a quarter of the satisfaction gap between managers and manual workers. Comparisons of job satisfaction between groups of workers therefore partly reflect who the workers are.
